newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Oman sign pacts but keep gas project on hold.
newsitem.headline: India, Oman sign pacts but keep gas project on hold.

text.p: India and Oman signed several agreements on Wednesday to boost bilateral cooperation but made little headway on a ambitious natural gas pipeline project linking the two countries.

The agreements, signed on the second day of a four-day visit to India by Oman's Sultan Qaboos Bin Said, included one on forming a joint venture company for a $1.1 billion fertiliser complex in the Gulf nation.
The agreements were signed after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Qaboos held talks on regional and international issues.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman said the talks covered cooperation between countries on the Indian Ocean Rim which have formed a regional economic grouping, and an exchange of views on the Middle East peace process.
Qaboos, accompanied by 14 ministers, arrived on Tuesday on a four-day visit, his first to a South Asian country.
The other agreements signed on Wednesday related to the avoidance of double taxation, investment protection and cooperation in civil aviation, agriculture and fisheries.

Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told reporters after the signing of agreements that the $4-billion Oman-India natural gas pipeline project has been put on hold in the absence of proper technology.
"For the time being, that project we are keeping it in abeyance till the technology is available," Gujral told reporters. "At the moment that technolgy is not available the world over," he said.
"The experts have to come out with the technical and economic feasibility findings. At the moment they are still looking at it," the Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Omani Minister for National Economy Ahmed Bin Abdul Nabi Macki, as telling a business meeting that the pipeline was not feasible.
"The project from our side is not viable as it is not beneficial to proceed with a project that is very risky," Macki said.
The two countries signed a memorandum of understanding in 1993 to build a pipeline running between the two nations under the Arabian Sea.
Omani officials said the Gulf state has spent $70 million to $80 million on the feasibility study and was not likely to spend any more on it.
According to the original plan, the proposed pipeline would be more than 1,300 km (813 miles) long and lie up to two miles under the ocean's surface.
The Fertiliser Ministry said the Oman-India Fertiliser Project (OIFP) would be among the biggest overseas ventures by Indian companies.

The joint venture agreement for setting up the Oman India Fertiliser Company was signed by Maqbool Bin Ali Bin Sultan, chairman of the Oman Oil Company, D.K. Verma, chairman of the state-run Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilisers Limited (RCF), and S. Kabilan, managing director of Krishak Bharati Cooperative Limited (KRIBHCO).

The project envisages the setting up of a world-class, ammonia-urea complex with an annual production capacity of 1.45 million tonnes of granulated urea and 330,000 tonnes of merchant ammonia at an estimated cost of $1.11 billion, officials said.
Oman will provide natural gas on a long-term basis and land for the project.
India will buy all of the urea production for 20 years under a buy-back arrangement at prices lower than international levels.
